title: Prompting & Structured Outputs

techniques.name: System Prompt Design
techniques.q: What does the model need to know before the first message?
techniques.what: The system prompt is the agent’s standing brief: who it is, what it is for, what it knows, the rules it must follow, when to use each tool, the exact output format, and what to do when it is unsure. Clear sections, explicit reasons for rules and no contradictions matter more than clever wording. Put stable text first so it can be cached, and variable data and the question last.
use: Every agent: it is the first thing to get right
Agents with several tools that are easy to confuse
Outputs that feed code, audits or customers
metrics: Role and goal
who the agent is, who it serves, what success looks like
Context
facts it needs, such as products, policies and dates
Rules and limits
what it must and must not do, with the reason
Tool guidance
when to use each tool and when not to
Output format
the exact structure, or a schema for structured outputs
Uncertainty
when to ask, refuse or escalate instead of guessing
steps: Write sections: role, context, rules, tools, format, uncertainty
Explain why each rule exists, and remove contradictions
Put stable text first and variables last, for caching and focus
Test on real cases and fix the failures, one change at a time
pitfalls: Rules added over months that now contradict each other
Vague instructions such as “be helpful” with no definition of done
Putting the user’s data before the instructions in long prompts, or timestamps at the top that break caching
techniques.remember: Say who, what, rules with reasons, tools, format, and what to do when unsure.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: a support agent’s accuracy with a vague prompt against a sectioned one.

techniques.name: Few-Shot Examples
techniques.q: Will examples help, or will the model copy them?
techniques.what: A few input–output examples in the prompt show the model the format, tone and decisions you want, often better than description alone. But models pick up whatever the examples share: the most common label, the last label, the length, even irrelevant surface features. Use a handful of diverse, balanced examples that cover edge cases, vary their order, and consider retrieving the most similar examples for each input.
use: Classification and extraction with subtle categories
A house style or format that is easier to show than describe
Edge cases the instructions alone keep getting wrong
metrics: Majority-label bias
the model over-predicts the label most examples share
Recency bias
the last example’s label is copied more often
Order sensitivity
the same examples in a different order can change results
Surface copying
length, phrasing or names in examples leak into outputs
Dynamic selection
retrieve the examples most similar to the current input
Token cost
each example is paid for on every call unless cached
steps: Start with instructions; add examples only where evals show a gap
Use 3–5 diverse examples with balanced labels, including an edge case
Rotate or randomise order, and wrap examples in tags
Measure accuracy and per-label prediction rates, not just the average
pitfalls: All examples sharing one label, so the model predicts it everywhere
Examples that contradict the written instructions
Dozens of static examples that cost tokens on every call
tools: Any vector store for example retrieval
techniques.remember: Few, diverse, balanced, shuffled. Measure per label.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: skewed examples double the predicted share of one label; balanced, retrieved examples raise accuracy.

cmp.best: The model copies the examples’ bias

techniques.name: JSON Schema and Constrained Decoding
techniques.q: Can I trust the shape of the output?
techniques.what: Asking for “JSON only” in the prompt still fails some of the time. JSON mode guarantees valid JSON but not your fields. Strict structured outputs go further: the decoder only allows tokens that keep the output valid against your JSON Schema, so the shape is guaranteed within the schema features the provider supports. The shape is not the truth: values can still be wrong, and some constraints, such as numeric ranges, must still be checked in code.
use: Any output that feeds code, a database or another tool
Extraction from documents into fixed fields
Tool arguments that must match a schema exactly
metrics: Prompt-only
“return JSON” in the prompt; occasional parse and field errors
JSON mode
always parseable JSON; fields and types not enforced
Strict schema
Anthropic output_config.format, OpenAI strict json_schema, strict tool use
OpenAI strict rules
additionalProperties false; every field required; optional fields allow null
Unsupported keywords
e.g. Anthropic: minimum, maximum, lengths and most regex patterns; validate these in code
Local models
constrained decoding with Outlines, XGrammar, llama.cpp grammars or vLLM structured outputs
steps: Define the output as a Pydantic model or JSON Schema
Use the provider’s strict structured-output mode or strict tools
Put a reasoning field before the answer fields when the task needs thought
Still validate values and business rules in code
pitfalls: Assuming a valid shape means correct values
Schemas so rigid that the model has no room to reason first
Relying on schema keywords the provider silently drops
techniques.remember: The schema guarantees the shape, not the truth.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: share of outputs matching an invoice schema under three modes.

cmp.needs: A schema and a supporting API

techniques.name: Validation and Repair Loops
techniques.q: What happens when the output is wrong?
techniques.what: Validate every structured output against types and business rules, such as a GSTIN format, totals that match their line items, or dates in range. When validation fails, send the specific error back to the model and ask for a corrected output, at most once or twice, then fall back: a human queue, a partial result or a clear failure. Generic “try again” retries waste calls; specific errors fix most problems in one round.
use: Outputs written to ledgers, CRMs or other systems of record
Extraction where some rules cannot be expressed in the schema
Pipelines that must never drop a record silently
metrics: Type validation
fields, types and enums, usually from the schema
Business rules
checksums, sums, cross-field consistency, allowed ranges
Specific feedback
the exact validation error goes back to the model
Retry cap
one or two repairs, then stop
Fallback
human queue or partial result; never a silent drop
Monitoring
track failure types to fix the prompt or schema at the source
steps: Encode rules as validators on a Pydantic model
On failure, return the validation errors to the model and ask for a fix
Cap retries at one or two; log every failure
Route unrepairable records to a human queue and review failure types weekly
pitfalls: Checking only types, so rule violations flow into the ledger
Retrying with the same prompt and no error message
Unlimited retries that multiply cost on hard inputs
techniques.remember: Validate rules, return the exact error, retry twice, then hand over.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: share of clean records after zero, one and three repair rounds with specific errors.

cmp.best: Silent errors in systems of record

techniques.name: Prompt Templates and Regression Tests
techniques.q: How do I change a prompt without breaking it?
techniques.what: Treat prompts as code. Build them from templates with named variables and shared blocks, fail loudly when a variable is missing, wrap untrusted variables in tags, and keep stable text before variable text. Every change runs a regression suite of golden cases in CI before it can ship, and versions are released through a registry, as AgentOps describes.
use: Prompts edited by several people or changed weekly
Many prompts sharing the same rules or policy text
Any prompt whose failures are costly
metrics: Template engine
Jinja2 or similar, with includes for shared blocks
Strict variables
StrictUndefined: a missing variable raises instead of rendering blank
Escaping
untrusted variables are wrapped in tags and escaped
Layout
stable text first for caching; variables and the question last
Golden cases
real inputs with expected outputs or graded criteria
CI gate
a change cannot merge unless the suite passes
steps: Move prompts into template files with named variables and shared includes
Render with strict undefined variables and wrap untrusted input
Build a golden set from real traffic, covering rare intents
Run it in CI on every prompt change, and block merges that regress
pitfalls: f-strings that silently render “None” when data is missing
A 20-case suite that misses rare intents
Editing prompts directly in production with no tests
techniques.remember: Prompts are code: templates, strict variables, tests in CI.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: the chance a change that breaks a 3% intent is caught, by suite size.

techniques.name: Prompting Reasoning Models
techniques.q: How should I prompt a model that thinks before it answers?
techniques.what: Reasoning models, such as Claude with extended thinking, OpenAI’s reasoning models and Gemini’s thinking models, already work through a problem in their own thinking tokens before they answer. Prompt them with the goal, the constraints and the checks a correct answer must pass, not a “think step by step” recipe; ask for the answer rather than the working; keep examples to a minimum; set the effort or thinking budget for each type of task; and send simple, latency-bound work to a non-reasoning model. How much thinking to buy is covered in Thinking budgets (Agent Architectures); this technique is about the prompt around it.
use: Multi-step work such as reconciliations, dispute analysis or code review on a reasoning model
Migrating prompts written for chat models, full of scaffolds and worked examples
Mixed traffic where cheap lookups and hard cases share one endpoint
metrics: Goals, not scaffolds
state the goal, the constraints and what “done” means; drop “think step by step”
Answer only
ask for the final answer or JSON; the thinking already happens in its own tokens
Self-checks
name the checks to run before answering, such as totals that must agree
Few-shot, sparingly
start zero-shot; add one or two examples only when the format needs showing
Effort per task
low effort or a small budget for routine tasks, high for multi-step ones
Right model
simple, latency-bound tasks go to a non-reasoning model
steps: Rewrite the prompt as goal, constraints, checks and output format
Remove step-by-step scaffolds, “show your working” and most worked examples
Set the effort or thinking budget per task type, with room left for the answer
Route simple lookups to a non-reasoning model and compare accuracy, cost and p95 latency
pitfalls: A fixed step-by-step recipe that overrides a better path the model would find on its own
Asking for the reasoning in the answer, paying for it twice and slowing every reply
One high effort setting for every request, so a balance lookup waits 20 seconds
techniques.remember: Say what and why, not how. Ask for the answer, and match the effort to the task.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: 10,000 tasks a day at RupeeRail, a fictional payment aggregator: 70% lookups and 30% settlement reconciliations.

cmp.scope: Slow, costly or worse answers from a thinking model
cmp.needs: Low: prompt edits and an effort setting per task
cmp.best: Scaffolds that fight the model’s own reasoning

techniques.name: Long-Context Prompting
techniques.q: How do I get reliable answers from a very long prompt?
techniques.what: How to prompt when the input is hundreds of pages: documents first, each wrapped in tags with its source, the question and instructions last, and a request to quote the relevant passages before answering. Long prompts are slow and expensive, so the shared prefix is cached, and retrieval is still the better choice when questions need only a few passages. Models also attend less reliably to the middle of very long inputs, so test on real multi-hop questions, not just needle-in-a-haystack checks.
use: Questions that span many parts of one long file: a loan bundle, a contract set, an annual report
Analysts asking many questions over the same documents
Multi-hop questions that retrieval of a few chunks tends to miss
metrics: Documents first
long inputs at the top, the question at the end
Tagged documents
each document in tags with source, date and page range
Quote first
ask for the relevant quotes, then the answer from them
Prompt caching
cache the shared prefix so later questions cost a fraction
Lost in the middle
facts buried mid-context are found less reliably
Stuff or retrieve
compare accuracy and cost against retrieving the top chunks
steps: Put long documents at the top, each in tags with its source and pages
Put the question and instructions at the end
Ask for the relevant quotes first, then an answer based only on them
Cache the document prefix, and compare with retrieval on your own multi-hop questions
pitfalls: Question at the top of 2,00,000 tokens of documents
Paying full input price for the same documents on every question
Trusting a needle-in-a-haystack score as proof of multi-hop reasoning
techniques.remember: Documents first, question last, quotes before answers.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Kosh Finance, a fictional NBFC, asks 50 questions over a 400-page loan bundle.

techniques.name: Multilingual Prompting (Hindi, Hinglish)
techniques.q: Will the prompt work when users write in Hindi or Hinglish?
techniques.what: Prompts and structured outputs for users who write in Hindi, Hinglish in Roman script, or another Indian language. Keep JSON keys and enum labels in English while values may be in any language, say explicitly which language and script to reply in, normalise spoken amounts and dates (“saadhe teen hazaar” → 3500), and include a code-mixed example or two. Measure accuracy per language slice, not only overall.
use: Support bots and assistants for Indian customers
Extraction of intents, amounts and dates from chat messages
Any prompt first written and tested only in English
metrics: English keys and enums
labels stay stable whatever the input language
Reply language
“reply in the user’s language and script” written into the prompt
Number normalisation
spoken or mixed amounts to digits in rupees
Code-mixed examples
one or two Hinglish and Hindi examples, not only English
Per-slice evaluation
accuracy for English, Hinglish and Hindi separately
Token cost
Devanagari often takes more tokens than Roman text; measure it
steps: Keep keys and enum labels in English, values in any language
Tell the model which language and script to reply in
Add rules and examples for amounts, dates and names in code-mixed text
Evaluate each language slice and fix the weakest first
pitfalls: Translating every message to English first and losing names and amounts
Enum labels that come back in Hindi and break the schema
Reporting one overall accuracy that hides a weak Hinglish slice
techniques.remember: English labels, the user’s language in replies, and test every slice.
techniques.cap: Illustrative: Kaveri Bank, a fictional bank, extracts intents and amounts from 1,000 messages in English, Hinglish and Hindi.

chooser: The agent behaves inconsistently or ignores rules
sysprompt
Rewrite the system prompt in sections, explain each rule, remove contradictions, and test.
It gets the format or subtle categories wrong
fewshot
Add a few diverse, balanced examples, shuffled or retrieved per input, and measure per label.
Outputs sometimes fail to parse or miss fields
schema
Use strict structured outputs with a JSON Schema or Pydantic model.
Outputs parse, but values break business rules
repair
Validate rules in code, send the exact error back, retry at most twice, then hand over.
Prompt edits keep breaking things
templates
Move prompts into templates with strict variables and run a golden-case suite in CI.
A reasoning model is slow and costly, and the prompt still says “think step by step”
reasonprompt
Replace the scaffold with goals, constraints and checks, ask for the answer only, set effort per task, and route simple lookups to a non-reasoning model.
Questions span a 400-page file and answers miss the details
longctx
Documents first with tags, question last, quotes before the answer, and a cached prefix.
Users write in Hindi and Hinglish and the JSON breaks
mlprompt
English keys and enums, an explicit reply language, amount rules, code-mixed examples, per-slice tests.

SYSTEM = """<role>
You are the billing support assistant for a mobile operator. You help         #@1
prepaid and postpaid customers understand charges and fix billing problems.  #@1
</role>
<rules>
- Never reveal another customer's data: verify the number belongs to the caller.  #@2
- Do not promise refunds above Rs 500, because only the billing team can approve them.  #@2
</rules>
<tools>
- get_bill: postpaid bills and itemised charges.                              #@3
- get_recharges: prepaid recharge history. Never use get_bill for prepaid.   #@3
</tools>
<format>
At most 4 short sentences, then one line: "Next step: ...".                  #@4
</format>
<when_unsure>
If the plan type is unclear, ask. If a tool fails twice, hand over to a human.  #@5
</when_unsure>"""

def reply(customer: str, question: str):
    return client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929", max_tokens=400,
        system=SYSTEM,                                   # stable, cacheable  #@6
        messages=[{"role": "user",                                            #@6
                   "content": f"<customer>{customer}</customer>\n{question}"}])  #@6
steps: State the role and the goal
Who the agent is, whom it serves and what a good outcome is. Without this, every later rule floats free of purpose.
Write rules with reasons
“Because only the billing team can approve them” lets the model handle refund cases the rule did not list. Rules without reasons get applied too literally or not at all.
Say when to use each tool
The two billing tools were being confused. One line each on what the tool is for, and one explicit “never”, fixes most tool-choice errors.
Pin down the format
A maximum length and a fixed final line make replies consistent and easy to check automatically.
Say what to do when unsure
Asking when the plan type is unclear, and handing over after two tool failures, replaces confident guesses with safe behaviour.
Stable first, variables last
The system prompt never changes between calls, so it can be cached. The customer’s details and question go in the message, last, where the model reads them just before answering.

import random
import numpy as np

EXAMPLES = load_labelled_examples()   # [{"text", "label", "vec"}] from real tickets  #@1
LABELS = ["refund", "delivery", "damage", "billing"]

def pick_examples(query_vec):
    chosen = []
    for label in LABELS:                                        # one per label   #@2
        pool = [e for e in EXAMPLES if e["label"] == label]                      #@2
        best = max(pool, key=lambda e: float(np.dot(e["vec"], query_vec)))       #@3
        chosen.append(best)                                                      #@3
    random.shuffle(chosen)                                      # no fixed order  #@4
    return chosen

def build_prompt(complaint: str, query_vec) -> str:
    shots = "\n".join(f"<example><text>{e['text']}</text><label>{e['label']}</label></example>"  #@5
                      for e in pick_examples(query_vec))                          #@5
    return (f"Classify the complaint as one of: {', '.join(LABELS)}.\n"
            f"<examples>\n{shots}\n</examples>\n<complaint>{complaint}</complaint>")  #@5

def label_rates(predictions):                                   # evaluate per label  #@6
    return {l: predictions.count(l) / len(predictions) for l in LABELS}          #@6
steps: Collect real, labelled examples
Examples come from real tickets with checked labels, including awkward ones. Invented examples tend to be too clean.
Balance the labels
One example per label means no label dominates. Four refunds out of five had pushed predicted refunds to 60%.
Pick the most similar
For each label, the example closest to this complaint is chosen, so the demonstrations are relevant to the case at hand.
Shuffle the order
The last example’s label gets copied more often. Shuffling removes a fixed recency bias.
Wrap examples in tags
Tags separate examples from instructions and from the real complaint, so the model does not confuse them.
Measure per label
Average accuracy can hide bias. Compare the share of each predicted label with the true share; a big gap means the model is copying the examples.

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class LineItem(BaseModel):                                                 #@1
    description: str                                                      #@1
    amount_inr: float                                                     #@1

class Invoice(BaseModel):                                                  #@1
    reasoning: str = Field(description="Where each total came from")       #@3
    gstin: str = Field(description="15-character GSTIN of the vendor")    #@2
    invoice_date: str = Field(description="ISO date, YYYY-MM-DD")         #@2
    items: list[LineItem]                                                  #@1
    total_inr: float                                                       #@1

client = Anthropic()

def extract(text: str) -> Invoice:
    r = client.messages.parse(model="claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929", max_tokens=1500,  #@4
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"<invoice>{text}</invoice>"}],        #@4
        output_format=Invoice)                  # strict JSON schema                 #@4
    if r.stop_reason == "max_tokens":                                              #@5
        raise RuntimeError("output truncated; raise max_tokens")                   #@5
    inv = r.parsed_output
    check_business_rules(inv)                   # shape is not truth              #@6

steps: Define the output as a model
A Pydantic model describes the fields and types. The SDK turns it into a JSON Schema for the API.
Describe fields, don’t rely on keywords
Constraints such as “15 characters” or date formats go in descriptions. Some schema keywords, like lengths and ranges, are not enforced and may be moved into descriptions by the SDK.
Let it reason first
A reasoning field before the numbers gives the model room to work out totals before committing to them. Very tight formats can otherwise cost accuracy.
Parse with the strict mode
messages.parse sends the schema through output_config.format; decoding is constrained, so the result always matches the model’s shape.
Handle truncation
If the response hit max_tokens, the object may be incomplete. Check the stop reason and raise the limit rather than trusting a cut-off answer.
Still check the values
Every field is present and typed, but a total can still disagree with its items. Business rules are checked next, in the repair loop.

from pydantic import ValidationError

def extract_with_repair(text: str, max_repairs: int = 2):
    messages = [{"role": "user", "content": f"<invoice>{text}</invoice>"}]
    last_error = None
    for attempt in range(max_repairs + 1):                                      #@4
        r = client.messages.parse(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1200,                 #@1
                                  messages=messages, output_format=InvoiceShape)  #@1
        try:
            return Invoice.model_validate(r.parsed_output.model_dump())         #@2
        except ValidationError as e:                                            #@2
            last_error = e
            log_failure(text, e.errors())                                       #@6
            messages += [{"role": "assistant", "content": r.content[0].text},   #@3
                         {"role": "user", "content":                            #@3
                          f"Fix these errors and return the whole invoice:\n{e}"}]  #@3
    queue_for_human(text, reason=str(last_error))                              #@5
    return None                                                                 #@5
steps: First attempt, strictly structured
The model returns an object that matches the schema’s shape, as in the previous technique.
Validate the business rules
Invoice adds validators: the GSTIN format and totals that match their items. 17% of first attempts fail one of them.
Send the exact error back
The model sees its own answer and the specific message, such as “total 11,800 does not match items summing to 11,200”. Most are fixed in one round.
Cap the repairs
At most two repairs. Hard inputs would otherwise loop and multiply the cost.
Hand over, never drop
If it still fails, the invoice goes to a human queue with the reason. Nothing invalid reaches the ledger, and nothing disappears.
Log failure types
Counting which rules fail most shows what to fix upstream: a clearer description, a schema change or a prompt rule.

steps: Prompts live in template files
Shared rules sit in one reviewed include used by every prompt, instead of being copied and drifting apart.
Missing variables fail loudly
With StrictUndefined, forgetting the ticket raises an error in tests rather than sending a prompt with a blank where the customer’s text should be.
Wrap and escape untrusted text
The ticket goes inside tags and is escaped, so it reads as data and cannot close the tag early.
Stable text first
The shared rules come first and never change between calls, which keeps the prefix cacheable; the ticket comes last.
Test against a golden set
300 real tickets with grading criteria. A change that breaks an intent seen in 3% of traffic is almost certainly covered.
Gate the merge in CI
Any change under prompts/ runs the suite. A failing case blocks the merge, before a version is ever promoted.

from itertools import product

STEPS = ["classify", "extract", "assess", "draft"]                           #@1
TIERS = {"S": ("claude-haiku-4-5-20251001", 0.02),                           #@2
         "M": ("claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929", 0.15),                          #@2
         "L": ("claude-opus-4-1-20250805", 0.90)}        # model, ₹ per call   #@2

SCORES = {s: {t: evaluate(s, model, EVALS[s])                                #@3
              for t, (model, _) in TIERS.items()} for s in STEPS}            #@3

def best_plan(min_e2e=0.85):
    plans = []
    for combo in product(TIERS, repeat=len(STEPS)):                          #@4
        acc = 1.0
        for s, t in zip(STEPS, combo):
            acc *= SCORES[s][t]                     # errors compound       #@4
        cost = sum(TIERS[t][1] for t in combo)                               #@5
        if acc >= min_e2e:                                                   #@5
            plans.append((cost, acc, combo))                                 #@5
    return min(plans)                               # cheapest that passes  #@5

# Re-run SCORES whenever a new model or snapshot arrives                   #@6
steps: Split the pipeline into steps
Classify, extract, assess and draft have very different difficulty; treating them as one hides that.
List the tiers with prices
Small, medium and large models with their cost per call. Model names here are examples.
Evaluate every step on every tier
Each step has its own small labelled eval set. Classification scores 97% even on the small model; assessment needs the large one for 94%.
Multiply step accuracies
Errors compound: 97% × 97.5% × 94% × 96% is 85.3% end to end. The weakest step limits the whole.
Take the cheapest plan that passes
Of 81 combinations, the cheapest above 85% end to end costs ₹1.97 a claim, against ₹3.60 for all-large.
Re-evaluate when models change
A new small model may pass a step that needed a large one. Rerunning the step evals is cheap; the savings compound.

import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
REASONING, FAST = "claude-sonnet-4-5", "claude-haiku-4-5"   # check current model ids

RECON = """Goal: reconcile today's UPI settlement file with RupeeRail's ledger.   #@1
Constraints: amounts are in paise; a refund can settle up to T+2;                 #@1
match a row only when both the UTR and the amount agree.                          #@1
Before you answer, check that matched + mismatched equals the rows in the file.   #@2
Reply with only this JSON: {"matched": int, "mismatches": [{"utr": str, "cause": str}]}"""  #@2

BUDGET = {"lookup": None, "recon": 8_000}   # thinking tokens per task type    #@3

def run(task_type: str, prompt: str, data: str):
    budget = BUDGET[task_type]
    if budget is None:                                                  #@5
        r = client.messages.create(model=FAST, max_tokens=300, system=prompt,  #@5
                                   messages=[{"role": "user", "content": data}])  #@5
        return r.content[0].text, r.usage                               #@5
    r = client.messages.create(
        model=REASONING,
        max_tokens=budget + 2_000,                 # room for the answer  #@4
        thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": budget},          #@3,4
        system=prompt,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": data}])
    answer = next(b.text for b in r.content if b.type == "text")      #@6
    return answer, r.usage           # output_tokens includes the thinking  #@6
steps: Goal and constraints, not a recipe

The prompt says what to achieve and which rules hold: paise, T+2 refunds, match only on UTR and amount. It does not say “think step by step” or number the steps. A reasoning model plans its own path, and a fixed recipe written for chat models often forces a worse one. There are no worked examples either: start zero-shot.
A check, and the answer only

Instead of asking for the working, the prompt names a check the answer must pass: matched plus mismatched equals the rows in the file. It then asks for the JSON alone. The model already reasons in its thinking tokens, so asking it to write the reasoning out again costs about 900 extra output tokens per reconciliation and adds nothing.
Effort per task type

Thinking is set per task type, not once for the whole service. A reconciliation gets 8,000 thinking tokens; a lookup such as “has UTR 4012… settled?” gets none. On Claude the budget is budget_tokens, at least 1,024; OpenAI uses reasoning.effort and Gemini a thinking budget or level.
Leave room for the answer

Thinking counts towards max_tokens, and budget_tokens must be below it. Setting max_tokens to the budget plus 2,000 leaves room for the JSON. Too little room means a rejected request or an answer cut off mid-way.
Send lookups to a fast model

Lookups need a record and one sentence, not a plan. They go to a fast model without thinking, answering in under a second at the 95th percentile instead of about 19 seconds, for about 2% of the cost, while accuracy drops only from 98.5% to 97.5%.
Read the answer, log the thinking

With thinking on, the response starts with a thinking block, so take the text block rather than content[0]. usage.output_tokens includes the thinking tokens, which are billed as output even when the visible thinking is summarised. Log it per task type to see where the money goes.

steps: Put the documents first, tagged
Each document goes in its own tags with its source file and page range, all above the question. The model can then say where a fact came from.
Ask the question last
A question placed after the documents is answered noticeably better than one placed before 2,50,000 tokens of text.
Quote before answering
The model first copies the clauses that matter into quotes, then answers from them alone. It cuts through the noise and leaves evidence you can check.
Cache the document prefix
Marking the documents for caching means the next 49 questions read them from cache at about a tenth of the input price, and much faster.
Check the quotes exist
Code confirms each quote appears in the cited document. A quote that cannot be found flags an invented clause.
Compare with retrieval
On your own questions, measure stuffing against retrieving the top chunks. Here stuffing wins on multi-hop questions; retrieval is cheaper for single facts.

from pydantic import BaseModel

class Ticket(BaseModel):                                               #@1
    intent: Literal["refund_status", "block_card", "kyc_update", "other"]   #@1
    amount_inr: int | None                                              #@1,3
    reply_lang: Literal["en", "hi-Deva", "hi-Latn"]                     #@2
    reply: str

SYSTEM = """Extract the ticket as JSON. Keys and intent labels stay in English.   #@1
Reply in the same language and script as the customer:                  #@2
Hinglish in Roman letters gets Hinglish, Hindi in Devanagari gets Devanagari.   #@2
Amounts: convert words to digits in rupees.                              #@3
"saadhe teen hazaar" = 3500, "dedh lakh" = 150000, "₹2.5k" = 2500.       #@3

Example: "mera card block karo, kho gaya"                                #@4
{"intent": "block_card", "amount_inr": null, "reply_lang": "hi-Latn",   #@4
 "reply": "Aapka card abhi block kar diya gaya hai."}"""                #@4

ticket = client.responses.parse(model=MODEL, instructions=SYSTEM,
                                input=message, text_format=Ticket).output_parsed

for lang, rows in eval_set.groupby("lang"):                             #@5,6
    print(lang, accuracy(rows), amount_accuracy(rows))                  #@5,6
steps: Keep keys and labels in English
The schema fixes the keys and the four intent labels. Whatever the customer writes, “refund_status” comes back spelled the same way, so the JSON validates.
Say which language to reply in
Without this line about one Hindi or Hinglish reply in five came back in English. Stating the language and the script fixes almost all of them.
Normalise amounts
Customers write “saadhe teen hazaar”, “3.5k” or “₹3,500”. A short rule with examples turns them all into 3500.
Show a code-mixed example
One Hinglish example teaches the pattern better than any English example. Hinglish intent accuracy rises from 78% to 90%.
Test each language separately
English at 95% can hide Hinglish at 78%. Report accuracy for every slice.
Fix the weakest slice first
Add examples and rules where the slice is weakest, then re-run all slices so English does not regress.

import random
import numpy as np

EXAMPLES = load_labelled_examples()        # [{"text": ..., "label": ..., "vec": np.array}]
LABELS = ["refund", "delivery", "damage", "billing"]

def pick_examples(query_vec, per_label=1):
    """Most similar example for each label: balanced and relevant."""
    chosen = []
    for label in LABELS:
        pool = [e for e in EXAMPLES if e["label"] == label]
        best = max(pool, key=lambda e: float(np.dot(e["vec"], query_vec)))
        chosen.extend([best][:per_label])
    random.shuffle(chosen)                  # no fixed order, no recency bias
    return chosen

def build_prompt(complaint: str, query_vec) -> str:
    shots = "\n".join(f"<example><text>{e['text']}</text><label>{e['label']}</label></example>"
                      for e in pick_examples(query_vec))
    return (f"Classify the complaint as one of: {', '.join(LABELS)}.\n"
            f"<examples>\n{shots}\n</examples>\n<complaint>{complaint}</complaint>")

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()
REASONING, FAST = "gpt-5-mini", "gpt-4.1-mini"   # examples: check current model names

INSTRUCTIONS = {
    # goal, constraints, one check, output format: no "think step by step"
    "recon": (
        "Goal: reconcile the UPI settlement file with the ledger.\n"
        "Constraints: amounts are in paise; refunds may settle up to T+2; "
        "match a row only when both the UTR and the amount agree.\n"
        "Before answering, check that matched + mismatched equals the rows in the file.\n"
        'Return only JSON: {"matched": int, "mismatches": [{"utr": str, "cause": str}]}'
    ),
    "lookup": "Answer the merchant's question from the record, in one sentence.",
}
EFFORT = {"recon": "high"}   # lookups skip reasoning entirely


def run(task_type: str, data: str) -> tuple[str, int]:
    if task_type not in EFFORT:                       # simple and latency-bound
        r = client.responses.create(model=FAST, instructions=INSTRUCTIONS[task_type],
                                    input=data, max_output_tokens=200)
        return r.output_text, 0
    r = client.responses.create(
        model=REASONING,
        reasoning={"effort": EFFORT[task_type]},
        instructions=INSTRUCTIONS[task_type],
        input=data,
        max_output_tokens=25_000,                     # reasoning tokens count against this
    )
    if r.status == "incomplete":                      # output room used up by reasoning
        raise RuntimeError(f"incomplete: {r.incomplete_details}")
    return r.output_text, r.usage.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens


if __name__ == "__main__":
    text, used = run("lookup", "UTR 401234567890: settled 26-09-2026, ₹4,999.00. Q: has it settled?")
    print(text, used)
    rows = open("settlement_2026-09-26.csv").read()
    text, used = run("recon", rows)
    print(f"reasoning tokens: {used:,}")
    print(text)

def pick_examples(query_vec, k=4):
    ranked = sorted(EXAMPLES, key=lambda e: -float(np.dot(e["vec"], query_vec)))
    chosen = ranked[:k]
    return chosen
fewshot.explain: Taking the top k most similar examples overall ignores labels, so a refund-like complaint gets four refund examples. The model then leans towards whatever label dominates, the majority-label bias the balanced design avoids.

reasonprompt.title: Reading the reconciliation result
reasonprompt.code:
def reconcile(data: str) -> dict:
    r = client.messages.create(
        model=REASONING, max_tokens=10_000,
        thinking={"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": 8_000},
        system=RECON, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": data}])
    answer = r.content[0].text
    return json.loads(answer)
reasonprompt.explain: With thinking enabled, the response starts with a thinking block and the answer comes after it, so content[0] is the thinking block, which has no text attribute. The call fails on every reconciliation, after paying for up to 8,000 thinking tokens.
reasonprompt.fix: answer = next(b.text for b in r.content if b.type == "text")

also.3: Correct: max_tokens leaves 2,000 tokens for the answer above the 8,000-token thinking budget.
also.4: Correct: budget_tokens is at least 1,024 and below max_tokens.

longctx.title: Building a long prompt
longctx.code:
def build(question, bundle):
    docs = "\n".join(f'<document source="{d.name}">\n{d.text}\n</document>' for d in bundle)
    return [
        {"type": "text", "text": f"Question: {question}\nQuote first, then answer."},
        {"type": "text", "text": f"<documents>\n{docs}\n</documents>",
         "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}},
    ]
longctx.explain: The question comes first, so the cached prefix changes with every question and nothing is ever reused; the model also reads 2,50,000 tokens before knowing what to look for. Put the documents block first and the question after it.
