sysprompt.q: Outline the sections of a system prompt for a customer-facing agent with tools, and say why each matters.
sysprompt.model: Start with the role and goal, so every rule has a purpose. Add stable context, then rules, each with its reason so the model can generalise. Say when to use each tool and when not to, which fixes most tool confusion. Specify the output format so replies are consistent and checkable, and say what to do when unsure: ask, refuse or hand over rather than guess. Keep stable text first for caching and put per-request data last.

sysprompt.q: A prompt has grown by accretion to 3,500 tokens and behaves erratically. How do you fix it?
sysprompt.model: Read it as a whole and list every rule; remove duplicates and resolve contradictions, since conflicting rules make the model choose unpredictably. Restructure the rest into sections with reasons, cut anything the model does correctly without being told, and move variable data out. Measure on a fixed test set before and after, so the rewrite is judged on results rather than impressions.

sysprompt.q: Why does the position of variable data in the prompt matter?
pts: end|last|near the question|lost in the middle
sysprompt.model: Providers cache a prompt’s prefix, so stable text must come first; a timestamp or user name at the top changes the prefix on every call and nothing is cached. For long inputs, putting documents first and the question last also tends to help the model use them, and information buried in the middle of long contexts is used less reliably.

fewshot.q: When do few-shot examples help, and how can they hurt?
pts: help with format and subtle decisions
fewshot.model: They help when a format, style or subtle category boundary is easier to show than describe, and when evals show instructions alone fall short. They hurt when the model copies patterns the examples share: the most common label, the last label, their length or wording. Order alone can change results, and every example costs tokens on each call.

fewshot.q: Design an example-selection scheme for a classifier with eight labels and 5,000 labelled tickets.
fewshot.model: Embed the labelled tickets. For each new ticket, retrieve the nearest examples, but pick at most one per label from the most relevant labels so no label dominates, and shuffle their order. Keep the number small, three to five, and evaluate on held-out tickets, checking accuracy and the predicted share of every label.

fewshot.q: Your few-shot classifier over-predicts one label. How do you diagnose it?
fewshot.model: Compare the share of each predicted label with its true share on held-out data. If one label is far over-predicted, look at the examples: count their labels and check which label comes last. Balance and shuffle them, or retrieve per label, and measure again.

schema.q: Compare prompt-only JSON, JSON mode and strict structured outputs.
pts: JSON mode: valid JSON, not your fields
schema.model: Asking for JSON in the prompt usually works but sometimes adds text or misses fields, so parsing can fail. JSON mode guarantees syntactically valid JSON but not which fields appear or their types. Strict structured outputs constrain decoding to your JSON Schema, so required fields are present with the right types, within the schema features the provider supports.

schema.q: Your strict schema output is always valid, but values are wrong 14% of the time. What would you do?
schema.model: Give the model room to think: add a reasoning field before the value fields, since very tight formats can cost accuracy. Put constraints and definitions in field descriptions, and validate business rules in code, sending failures back for repair. Measure value accuracy separately from schema validity.

schema.q: What limits of structured outputs should an engineer know?
schema.model: Providers support a subset of JSON Schema: for example ranges, lengths and most patterns may not be enforced, and there are limits on optional and union fields. The schema guarantees the shape, not correct content. A response can still be cut off at max_tokens or refused, so check the stop reason or refusal field before using the object.

repair.q: Design a repair loop for extraction into a system of record.
repair.model: Define business rules as validators on the output model. On failure, send the model its answer and the exact validation errors and ask for a corrected, complete output. Cap repairs at one or two, log every failure with its type, and route anything still invalid to a human queue with the reason. Only validated records are written.

A generic retry repeats the same prompt under the same conditions, so the model often makes the same mistake again and each attempt costs a call. It carries no information about what was wrong; a specific validation error tells the model exactly what to fix.

repair.q: How do you use repair-loop failures to improve the system over time?
repair.model: Log each validation failure with its type and input. Review the counts regularly: the most common failures point to upstream fixes, such as a clearer field description, a schema change, a prompt rule or a pre-processing step. Add those cases to the regression suite so the fix stays fixed.

templates.q: What does “treat prompts as code” mean in practice?
templates.model: Prompts live in version-controlled template files with named variables and shared includes, render with strict undefined variables so missing data fails, and are reviewed like code. Every change runs a golden-case regression suite in CI, and released versions are promoted through a registry, so any change is tested, reversible and attributable.

templates.q: How large should a golden set be?
templates.model: Large enough to cover the intents you cannot afford to break. For an intent in 3% of traffic, random sampling needs about 100 cases for a 95% chance of including it, and 300 for near certainty. Add rare intents deliberately rather than relying on sampling, and add every past incident as a case.

templates.q: Why escape and wrap untrusted variables in templates?
pts: untrusted text can contain instructions or tags
templates.model: Variables such as tickets or documents come from users or third parties and can contain instructions or text that closes your tags. Wrapping them in clear tags and escaping them keeps them marked as data and preserves the prompt’s structure. It is not a complete defence against injection, but it removes easy mistakes.

reasonprompt.q: How would you rewrite a chat-model prompt for a reasoning model, and why?
reasonprompt.model: Replace the recipe with the goal, the constraints and the checks a correct answer must pass, then the exact output format. Remove “think step by step”, numbered procedures and requests to show the working: the model already reasons in its own thinking tokens, and a fixed path can make it worse. Start zero-shot, adding an example only if the format needs showing. Set the effort or thinking budget per task type, and compare the new prompt with the old on the same eval set.

reasonprompt.q: 7,000 lookups a day cost ₹1.513 each on a reasoning model at high effort, or ₹0.028 each on a fast model, with accuracy falling from 98.5% to 97.5%. What is the daily saving, and is it worth it? Show the working.
reasonprompt.model: Per lookup: ₹1.513 − ₹0.028 = ₹1.485. Per day: 7,000 × ₹1.485 = ₹10,395, about ₹3,11,850 a month. The cost is 1 point of lookup accuracy, 70 more wrong answers a day, while p95 latency falls from about 19 seconds to under 1. For a customer-facing lookup that is usually worth it; check that the extra errors are recoverable, for example by falling back on low confidence.

reasonprompt.q: After moving to a reasoning model, reconciliation accuracy fell from 93% to 89% and every reply now opens with a long explanation. What happened, and what would you change?
pts: the old scaffold forces a path
reasonprompt.model: The prompt still carries the chat-model scaffold: a numbered procedure, worked examples and “show your working”. On a reasoning model the recipe overrides the better path the model would plan itself, and the written-out working is paid output that adds latency. Rewrite the prompt as goal, constraints, a self-check and JSON only, keep effort high for reconciliations, and compare both prompts on the same labelled set before switching.

longctx.q: Explain how you would prompt a model to answer questions over a 400-page loan file.
longctx.model: Put the documents first, each in tags with its source and page range, and the question at the end. Ask the model to copy the relevant clauses into quotes and answer only from them, then check the quotes exist. Cache the document prefix so repeated questions cost a fraction, and compare against retrieval on your own questions.

longctx.q: The bundle is 2,50,000 tokens at ₹0.25 per 1,000, and cached reads cost a tenth. What do 50 questions cost with and without caching?
longctx.model: Without caching: 50 × ₹62.5 = ₹3,125. With caching: ₹62.5 for the first question plus 49 × ₹6.25 = ₹306.25, so ₹368.75 in total.

longctx.q: Accuracy is fine on single facts but poor on questions that need two clauses from different documents. What do you try?
longctx.model: These are multi-hop questions: the answer needs passages far apart, which a small top-k retrieval often misses and which get lost in the middle of a long prompt. Put the whole bundle in with the question last, ask for quotes from each document before answering, and measure multi-hop accuracy separately.

mlprompt.q: How would you make a JSON extraction prompt work for Hindi and Hinglish users?
mlprompt.model: Fix keys and intent labels in English with a schema, tell the model to reply in the customer’s language and script, add rules and examples for amounts and dates, include Hinglish and Hindi examples, and report accuracy for each language.

mlprompt.q: English 95% on 400, Hinglish 90% on 300, Hindi 92% on 300. What is overall accuracy?
After launch, Hindi users complain that amounts are wrong though overall accuracy is 94%. Diagnose.
mlprompt.model: The overall figure hides a weak Hindi slice. Amounts written as words, such as “dedh lakh” or “saadhe teen hazaar”, are misread. Add normalisation rules and examples, and track amount accuracy per language.

cases.title: The invoice extractor that breaks the ledger
cases.brief: An Indian NBFC uses an agent to read vendor invoices and post them to its ledger: GSTIN, invoice number, date, line items and total. Finance has found wrong entries during reconciliation, and the monthly model bill keeps growing. You are asked which techniques to apply first, and in what order.
evidence: 6% of outputs fail to parse. The prompt says “return JSON only”, and on failure the pipeline retries the whole call, with the same prompt, up to five times.
Of the outputs that parse, about 4% have totals that do not match their line items or GSTINs in the wrong format, and they are posted to the ledger.
The system prompt has grown to 3,500 tokens of rules added after incidents; two of them contradict each other on rounding paise.
Every step, including a simple “is this document an invoice?” check, runs on the largest model.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Then compare with the model answer.

why.schema: Start here. Strict structured outputs from a Pydantic model remove the 6% parse failures and the blind five-fold retries at once, which is the quickest fix to both errors and cost.
why.repair: Schemas cannot check that totals match items or that a GSTIN is well formed. Business-rule validators, the exact error sent back for at most two repairs, and a human queue stop the 4% of bad entries reaching the ledger.
why.sysprompt: The contradiction on rounding paise makes the model pick one rule at random. Rewriting the prompt in sections, with reasons and no conflicts, also shrinks 3,500 tokens that are paid on every call.
why.tiering: Useful once correctness is fixed: the invoice check and simple fields do not need the largest model. Evaluating each step and moving the easy ones to a smaller tier cuts the bill further.
why.fewshot: Not needed: the errors are about shape, arithmetic and contradictory rules, not subtle categories or style that examples would teach.
why.templates: Not needed first: there is one prompt with no variable-rendering failures reported. Adding a regression suite is good practice after the rewrite, but it does not fix today’s errors.
why.reasonprompt: Not needed: reading fields off an invoice is not multi-step work. Moving to a thinking model would add cost and latency to a pipeline whose problems are shape, arithmetic and a contradictory rule.
why.longctx: Not needed: an invoice is a page or two. Document-first layout and quote-before-answer solve a problem this pipeline does not have.
why.mlprompt: Not needed on this evidence: no language slice appears in it. Worth measuring separately if vendors start submitting Hindi or regional-language invoices, but it fixes none of the four symptoms.

firstWhy.sysprompt: Defensible — the contradiction is real — but you would spend the sprint on wording while 6% of invoices still fail to parse and bad totals keep posting. Fix what code can check first.
firstWhy.tiering: This is the cost symptom, and it is the cheapest to fix last. Move steps to smaller models while 4% of entries are wrong and you make a wrong answer cheaper, not right.
firstWhy.repair: Close. But validators run on outputs you can parse, and 6% of yours cannot be parsed at all. Guarantee the shape first, then check the values.

cases.model: Start with strict structured outputs: define the invoice as a Pydantic model and use the provider’s strict schema mode, which removes the 6% parse failures and the five blind retries at once. Next, add business-rule validators for totals and GSTIN format; on failure, send the exact error back for at most two repairs, and route anything still invalid to a human queue so nothing wrong reaches the ledger. Then rewrite the system prompt in sections, resolving the paise-rounding contradiction and cutting the accumulated 3,500 tokens, with stable text first so it can be cached. Finally, evaluate each step separately and move the invoice check and other easy steps to a smaller model. Few-shot examples do not address these errors, and a template regression suite is worth adding after the rewrite rather than before.
cases.note: Fix the shape first, then the values, then the instructions that caused them, and only then the cost. Case 2 looks similar and needs almost the opposite answer — try it before you accept that order as a rule.

schema: Symptom 1 says 6% of outputs cannot be parsed at all, and the pipeline answers by sending the same prompt five more times. What on this page makes the shape of an output something you can rely on, rather than something you ask for politely?
Asking for JSON in words is a request. Something here turns it into a constraint the decoder cannot break, and it acts while the model is writing rather than after it has finished.
JSON Schema and Constrained Decoding. Read what it guarantees — and the line about what it does not.
repair: Symptom 2: the totals do not match their line items, and these outputs parse perfectly. What checks that a number is right, rather than that it is a number?
Something that runs after the model has answered, compares it against rules you wrote yourself, and decides whether to ask again or hand the case to a person.
Validation and Repair Loops. Note what it does when the second repair also fails.
sysprompt: Symptom 3: two rules in the prompt contradict each other on rounding paise. What does a model do when its own instructions disagree, and what fixes that?
This one is not about the output at all. It is about the standing brief the model reads before every message — 3,500 tokens of it, paid for on every call.
System Prompt Design. Look at the sections it asks for, and why every rule needs its reason attached.

drop.fewshot: Examples teach subtle categories and house style. Which of the four symptoms is about a category or a style?
drop.templates: A regression suite protects you from changes you make. Is any symptom here caused by a prompt edit?
drop.reasonprompt: A thinking model earns its cost on multi-step work. Is reading fields off an invoice multi-step work — and what would it do to the bill that is already a symptom?
drop.longctx: An invoice is a page or two. Which symptom is about the length of the prompt?
drop.mlprompt: Which of the four symptoms mentions a language?

cases.firstHint: You have the right techniques. Now ask which of them the other two depend on: until one of your steps is done, 6% of outputs cannot even be read, so nothing about them can be measured.

whyFirst.q: Before you check — which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: The system prompt is the largest number in the evidence, at 3,500 tokens.
6% of outputs cannot be parsed at all, so nothing about them can be measured until that is fixed.
The model bill grows every month, and cost compounds faster than errors do.
whyFirst.why: Order follows what you can verify. Totals, rules and wording can all be argued about; an output your code cannot parse is not in dispute, and fixing it also removes the five blind retries sitting behind it.

cases.title: The triage agent nobody trusts
cases.brief: A health insurer routes inbound customer messages — WhatsApp, app chat and email — into one of nine queues (pre-authorisation, claim status, network hospital, grievance and so on) and drafts the first reply. Operations says the agent is confidently wrong, and the grievance team is the loudest. You are asked to fix the quality. Note what is not in the evidence as carefully as what is.
evidence: Every output parses and matches its schema. There has not been a single format incident in three months.
18% of messages reach the wrong queue. Grievances are the worst: nearly a third are filed as claim-status questions, because in one line the two read alike.

Accuracy on Hindi and Hinglish messages is 61% against 83% on English, and the agent sometimes replies in English to a customer who wrote in Hindi. Nobody had measured the two slices separately until last week.
The drafted replies swing in tone from curt to over-apologetic. Three people have each edited the tone paragraph in the last month, and nobody can say which wording is live.
A grievance about a hospital refusing cashless treatment needs three facts combined before it can be classified. The agent answers in one step and gets it wrong.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. One piece of evidence is there to rule a technique out rather than to be fixed.

why.fewshot: Grievance against claim status is exactly the subtle distinction instructions keep getting wrong and examples teach quickly. Take a few real messages per queue, balanced across the nine so the model does not learn the volume split, shuffled, and measure accuracy per queue rather than overall. The same technique settles the reply tone: house style is easier to show than to describe.
why.mlprompt: A 22-point gap between English and Hindi is a hidden slice, not a general accuracy problem, and it stayed hidden because nobody split the eval set. Keep the queue labels in English inside the prompt, state that the reply must be in the language the customer wrote in, and hold a test set per slice — English, Hindi, Hinglish — from here on.
why.templates: Three people editing a tone paragraph with no record of what is live is the whole problem in one sentence. One template with named variables, the prompt under version control, and a golden set of messages in CI turns every later change into something you can measure instead of argue about.
why.reasonprompt: Useful for the hard tail: the cashless-refusal grievance needs several facts combined, which is what a thinking model is for. Say what to decide and why it matters rather than scripting the steps, and reserve the higher effort setting for messages the first pass marks as unclear — not for all nine queues.
why.sysprompt: Useful, and partly unavoidable: the queue definitions and the tone rule live in the system prompt, so the template work will rewrite it anyway. On its own it is not the fix — the two queues are genuinely hard to tell apart in one line, and more prose about the difference is what has been tried so far.
why.schema: Not needed, and the first piece of evidence is there to tell you so. The output is already a strict schema, every response parses, and no format incident has occurred in three months. A schema guarantees the shape of an answer; it has nothing to say about whether the answer is right. This is the case where the quickest fix from case 1 does nothing at all.
why.repair: Not needed: a validator can only check a rule you can state, and “this is a grievance, not a claim-status question” is a judgment, not a rule. The one checkable assertion here — that the reply language matches the message language — is worth adding as a line of code, but it is not the technique that moves 18% wrong routing.
why.longctx: Not needed: these are chat messages of a few lines each. There is no long document to lay out and no position effect to defend against.
why.tiering: Not needed here, and the wrong moment for it. Cost appears nowhere in the evidence, and moving a routing step that is already 18% wrong to a smaller model would make it worse. Revisit it after accuracy is fixed — in case 1 it was the right kind of useful; here it is a distraction.

firstWhy.fewshot: The right technique, a step early. Change the examples now and you will not be able to show what moved — there is no golden set, and three people are still editing the prompt underneath you.
firstWhy.sysprompt: More prose about the difference between a grievance and a claim-status question is what has been tried for three months. The distinction needs examples, and the edits need a version you can point at.
firstWhy.schema: Nothing here is a shape problem. Every output already parses and matches its schema — that is the first thing the evidence tells you.

cases.model: Nothing is broken in a way code can see, so the first move is to make change measurable: one template with named variables, under version control, and a golden set of real messages per queue in CI. Then split the eval set by language, because a 22-point Hindi gap is a slice problem and an overall number hides it; fix the reply-language rule at the same time. With a baseline in place, add a few balanced, shuffled examples per queue — especially grievance against claim status — and judge them per queue rather than on the average, using the same examples to pin the reply tone. Finally, route the genuinely multi-fact grievances to a reasoning model at a higher effort setting, and leave the other eight queues where they are. Structured outputs, validators, long-context layout and model tiering all address problems this system does not have; tiering in particular would be actively harmful while routing is still 18% wrong.
cases.note: Compare this with case 1. Same module, same eight techniques, and the technique that fixed everything there fixes nothing here. The question is never “which technique is best” — it is which symptom you actually have, and whether you can measure a change before you make it.

templates: Symptom 4: three people have each edited the tone paragraph this month and nobody can say which wording is live. Before you change anything else, what makes a change to a prompt something you can point at afterwards?
Treat the prompt the way you treat code: one version, named variables, and a set of known messages that runs on every edit.
Prompt Templates and Regression Tests. Note what the golden set is for.
mlprompt: Symptom 3: 61% on Hindi and Hinglish against 83% on English, and nobody had split the two until last week. What kind of problem hides inside a single overall accuracy number?
The fix is half in the prompt — which language the labels are in, and which language the reply must be in — and half in how you test: one slice at a time.
Multilingual Prompting. Look at what it says about English labels and the user’s language.
fewshot: Symptom 2: nearly a third of grievances are filed as claim-status questions, because in one line the two read alike. Three months of clearer instructions have not moved it. What works better than describing a distinction?
Show rather than tell — and watch the balance, or the model learns your queue volumes instead of your categories.
Few-Shot Examples. Note why they must be balanced, shuffled, and measured per label rather than on the average.

drop.schema: Read symptom 1 again. Every output already parses and matches its schema, and there has been no format incident in three months. What would adding one change?
drop.repair: A validator checks a rule you can state. Can you state the rule that separates a grievance from a claim-status question?
drop.longctx: These are chat messages of a few lines each. Which symptom is about length?
drop.tiering: Cost appears nowhere in this evidence. And if a routing step is already 18% wrong, what does moving it to a smaller model do to it?

cases.firstHint: You have the right techniques. Now ask what you would have to do before changing any of them, given that three people are editing the prompt and nobody knows which version is live.

whyFirst.q: Before you check — which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: The grievance team is the loudest complaint, so their queue should be fixed first.
Hindi accuracy is the largest single gap in the evidence, at 22 points.
Nothing here is broken in a way code can see, so the first move is to make a change something you can measure.
whyFirst.why: In case 1 the first move was to fix the output, because the output was broken. Here every output is fine and what is missing is a baseline. Change the examples before you have one and you will not be able to show whether the 18% moved at all.

cases.title: The prompt that worked in a notebook
cases.brief: A bank’s credit team has an assistant that answers questions about loan files: a 60- to 200-page bundle per borrower — sanction letter, bank statements, CA-certified financials, legal opinion. One analyst built it in a notebook and it worked well. Six months on, four people edit the prompts, there are forty-odd variants in a shared folder, and the credit committee has stopped trusting the answers. Nothing crashes. The answers are just unreliable in ways nobody can pin down.
evidence: The assistant finds a fact reliably when it sits on the first or last pages of the bundle and misses it when the same fact sits in the middle — same question, same file, different page.

The prompt is assembled with f-strings in four places. Last Tuesday a missing variable rendered the text “None” into the policy section, and the assistant answered with no policy at all for two days before anyone noticed.
There is no record of which prompt produced which answer. When the committee challenged a rejection, nobody could reproduce it.
Every question re-sends the whole bundle, and the same bundle is asked twenty to thirty questions during underwriting. The monthly bill is now the team’s largest line item after salaries.
The “is this page a bank statement or a financial statement?” classification step runs on the largest model, two hundred times a day.
cases.task: Choose the techniques you would apply, put them in order, and say which symptom each one fixes. Two of these symptoms are not about the model’s ability at all.

why.templates: Two of the five symptoms are assembly failures, not model failures. f-strings in four places silently rendered “None” into a policy section, and no answer can be traced to the prompt that produced it. One template per task with strict variables that fail loudly on a missing value, the prompt version recorded with every answer, and a golden set of committee questions in CI — that is what makes the other fixes measurable and the rejection defensible.
why.longctx: The first symptom is the classic position effect: a fact in the middle of a long prompt gets less attention than the same fact at either end. Put the documents first and the question last, ask for the supporting quotes before the answer so a citation can be checked, and cache the bundle prefix instead of re-sending 200 pages for every one of thirty questions — which also takes a large bite out of the bill.
why.tiering: “Is this page a bank statement?” is a two-way classification running two hundred times a day on the largest model available. Split the pipeline into steps, evaluate every step on every tier, multiply the step accuracies, and take the cheapest plan that still passes. Here it is essential rather than merely useful, because cost is one of the reported symptoms and not a side effect.
why.sysprompt: Useful, and the template work will force it: forty variants in a shared folder collapse into one brief with sections — role, the policy facts, the rules with their reasons, the citation format, and what to do when the bundle does not answer the question. Do it as part of the consolidation, not as a separate project before it.
why.reasonprompt: Useful once the plumbing is trustworthy. “Does the declared turnover match the bank statements?” is multi-step work across several documents, which is what a thinking model is for — say what to decide and why, and keep the higher effort setting for the committee-facing questions rather than every lookup.
why.schema: Not needed: the deliverable is a paragraph a credit officer reads, not an object code consumes. The one part worth making structured — which page each claim came from — is better handled by asking for quotes before the answer, which is part of long-context layout.
why.repair: Not needed: nothing is being written to a system of record and no stated rule is being broken. The answers are unreliable, not invalid, and a validator has nothing to check. Compare case 1, where 4% of outputs broke rules you could write down — that is what repair loops are for.
why.fewshot: Not needed: the failures are about where text sits in the prompt and which prompt ran, not about subtle categories or house style. Examples would add tokens to a prompt that is already too long, and make the position problem slightly worse.
why.mlprompt: Not needed: the bundle and the questions are in English, and no language slice appears in the evidence.

firstWhy.longctx: The right technique, and tempting because the position effect is the most interesting symptom. But rearrange the prompt while it is still assembled by f-strings in four places, with no record of which version ran, and you cannot show that your change helped.
firstWhy.tiering: Cost is a real symptom here, but step evals are only meaningful once you know which prompt each step is running. Make the pipeline knowable, then make it cheap.
firstWhy.sysprompt: Consolidating forty variants is exactly right — but it is the template work, and doing it by hand without strict variables and a golden set leaves you with variant forty-one.

cases.model: Start with the plumbing, because two of the five symptoms are not about the model at all: one template per task with strict variables that raise on a missing value instead of rendering “None”, the prompt version recorded alongside every answer, and a golden set of committee questions in CI. Then fix the layout: documents first and the question last, quotes before answers so every claim can be traced to a page, and the bundle prefix cached rather than re-sent for each of thirty questions. Then split the pipeline and evaluate each step on each tier — the bank-statement classification does not need the largest model two hundred times a day — and take the cheapest plan that still passes. The forty prompt variants collapse into one sectioned brief as part of the template work, and multi-document questions such as whether declared turnover matches the bank statements are worth moving to a reasoning model once the rest is trustworthy. Structured outputs, repair loops, examples and multilingual work all target problems this system does not have.
cases.note: Three cases, three different first moves: fix the output, make the change measurable, make the system knowable. What they share is not an order of techniques — it is that the first move always goes to the symptom you can verify, not the one that is most interesting to work on.

templates: Symptoms 2 and 3 are not about the model’s ability at all. An f-string rendered the text “None” into a policy section for two days, and no answer can be traced to the prompt that produced it. What makes a prompt reproducible?
Strict variables that fail loudly instead of rendering text, the version recorded alongside every answer, and a known set of questions that runs on every change.
Prompt Templates and Regression Tests. Note what it says about variables that are missing at render time.
longctx: Symptom 1: the same fact is found on the first or last pages and missed in the middle. That is not randomness. What property of a very long prompt causes it, and what do you do about it?
Where a document sits inside the prompt changes how much attention it gets. There is also a reason not to re-send 200 pages for each of thirty questions.
Long-Context Prompting. Note the order it asks for, and what caching the prefix does to symptom 4.
tiering: Symptom 5: a two-way “is this a bank statement or a financial statement?” check runs on the largest model two hundred times a day. What should you be asking about every step of a pipeline separately?
Not every step needs the same model, and the way to find out is to measure each step on each tier rather than to guess.
Model Tiering. Note that you multiply the step accuracies together before choosing a plan.

drop.schema: The deliverable is a paragraph a credit officer reads. Which symptom is about a shape that code has to consume?
drop.repair: Nothing is being written to a system of record and no stated rule is being broken. What would your validator check?
drop.fewshot: The failures are about where text sits in the prompt and which prompt ran. What would more examples do to a prompt that is already too long?

cases.firstHint: The right techniques. Now ask which of your steps the other two cannot be measured without, given that nobody can say which prompt produced which answer.

whyFirst.q: Before you check — which is the strongest reason for a step to go first in this case?
options: Two of the five symptoms are assembly failures, and until the pipeline is knowable no other fix can be shown to have worked.
The position effect is the most interesting symptom, and the only one unique to long prompts.
Cost is now the team’s largest line item after salaries, so it compounds for as long as it is left.
whyFirst.why: The committee’s actual complaint is that nothing can be reproduced. A better layout and cheaper models are both worth having, but neither is defensible while the prompt that produced an answer is unknown.

tiering: Does every step need the biggest model?

sysprompt.t: A system prompt has 1,230 tokens of stable text and 60 tokens of per-request data. The data is moved from the top to the end, so the stable prefix can be cached. With cache reads at 0.1× the input price, what share of the prompt’s input cost remains per call, in percent? (Ignore the one-off cache write.)
sysprompt.a: Cached: 1,230 × 0.1 = 123 token-equivalents; uncached: 60. Total 183 of 1,290, or about 14.2% of the original input cost. Putting the variable data at the top would break the cache on every call.
iv: What belongs in a system prompt, and what does not?

It holds the standing brief: role and goal, stable context, rules with reasons, tool guidance, output format and what to do when unsure. Per-request data such as the customer’s details and the question belong in the messages, after the stable text, so the prompt stays cacheable and the model sees the question last.
Why explain the reason for a rule?

A reason lets the model apply the rule to cases the wording did not anticipate and weigh it against other rules. “Never promise refunds above ₹500 because only the billing team can approve them” generalises better than “no refunds above ₹500”.
mis: Adding rules for every incident until they contradict
Review the prompt as a whole and remove conflicts
Putting a timestamp or user name at the top
Keep variable data at the end so the prefix can be cached

fewshot.t: True complaint labels are 30% refund, 30% delivery, 20% damage and 20% billing. With skewed examples the model predicts refund for 60% of complaints. If every true refund is still labelled refund, what share of all complaints is wrongly labelled refund, in percent?
fewshot.a: 60% predicted refund minus 30% that really are refunds leaves 30% of all complaints wrongly labelled refund. Those errors come from the other labels, so accuracy can fall by up to 30 points.
iv: Why can few-shot examples make a model worse?

Models pick up patterns the examples share, including ones you did not intend: the most common label, the label of the last example, their length or their wording. Skewed or unrepresentative examples bias outputs towards them. Balanced, diverse examples in varied order avoid this.
When should you retrieve examples dynamically?

When the input space is broad and a fixed handful cannot cover it, or when the best example depends on the input. Retrieving the most similar labelled examples for each input, balanced across labels, gives relevant demonstrations without paying for dozens of static ones on every call.
mis: Using the first five examples you found
Choose diverse, balanced examples that include edge cases
Always putting the same example last
Shuffle or rotate the order

schema.t: An extractor processes 50,000 invoices a month. With “JSON only” in the prompt, 6% fail to parse and each is retried once at ₹0.40. How much a month do those retries cost?
schema.a: 6% of 50,000 is 3,000 retries × ₹0.40 = ₹1,200 a month, plus the delay and the retries that fail again. Strict structured outputs remove parse failures entirely, though value checks still apply.
iv: What is the difference between JSON mode and strict structured outputs?

JSON mode guarantees syntactically valid JSON but not which fields appear or their types. Strict structured outputs constrain decoding to your JSON Schema, so every required field is present with the right type, within the schema features the provider supports.
If the output matches the schema, why validate it again?

A schema guarantees the shape, not the correctness of values. An invoice can have a well-formed total that does not match its items, or a GSTIN that is a string but not a valid one. Some constraints, such as ranges and patterns, may not be enforced by the provider at all, so business rules must be checked in code.
mis: Asking for JSON in the prompt and parsing with try/except
Use the provider’s strict structured-output mode
Putting the answer before any reasoning in a tight schema
Add a reasoning field first when the task needs thought

repair.t: 17.2% of first outputs fail validation. Each repair with the specific error succeeds 70% of the time. With up to two repairs, what share of records still fails, in percent?
repair.a: 17.2% × 0.3 × 0.3 = 1.55%. One repair leaves 5.2%, two leave 1.55%, and a third would leave about 0.46%. Those go to a human queue rather than the ledger.
iv: Why send the validation error back rather than just retrying?

A plain retry repeats the same conditions, so the model often makes the same mistake. The specific error, such as “total 11,800 does not match items summing to 11,200”, tells it exactly what to fix, and most outputs are corrected in one round.
What should happen when repairs run out?

Stop and hand over: put the record in a human queue with the error, or return a partial result marked as incomplete. Never write an invalid record to a system of record, and never drop it silently. Track failure types to fix the prompt or schema at the source.
mis: Retrying until it passes, with no cap
Cap repairs at one or two, then fall back
Validating only types
Add business-rule validators: sums, checksums, dates

templates.t: A prompt change breaks an intent that makes up 3% of traffic. Your golden suite has 100 cases sampled from traffic. What is the chance that at least one case covers that intent, in percent?
templates.a: 1 − 0.97¹⁰⁰ ≈ 1 − 0.048 = 95.2%. With 20 cases it is only 45.6%; with 300 it is over 99.9%. Rare intents need bigger suites or deliberate coverage.
iv: Why use StrictUndefined in Jinja2 prompt templates?

By default a missing variable renders as an empty string, so a prompt can silently lose the customer’s data or a policy block. StrictUndefined raises an error at render time, which tests and CI catch before release.
How do you build a good golden set for prompt regression tests?

Sample real inputs from production across intents, deliberately add rare but important cases and past failures, and write assertions or rubrics for each. Keep it versioned, grow it whenever an incident reveals a gap, and run it in CI on every prompt change.
mis: Editing prompts with f-strings and no tests
Use templates with strict variables and a CI suite
A golden set of only easy, common cases
Include rare intents and past failures

reasonprompt.t: A reconciliation on a reasoning model reads 3,400 input tokens, thinks for 9,000 tokens and writes a 400-token answer. Input costs ₹170 per million tokens and output ₹850 per million, with thinking billed as output. What does one reconciliation cost, in rupees?
reasonprompt.a: Input: 3,400 × ₹0.00017 = ₹0.578. Output: (9,000 + 400) × ₹0.00085 = ₹7.99. Total ₹8.568, about ₹8.57, and ₹7.65 of it (89%) is thinking. Asking for another 900 tokens of written-out working would add ₹0.77 per reconciliation, ₹2,295 a day at 3,000 reconciliations.
iv: How does prompting a reasoning model differ from prompting a chat model?

The model already plans and checks in its own thinking tokens, so step-by-step scaffolds, “show your working” and long worked examples are unnecessary and can make results worse by forcing a fixed path. Give the goal, the constraints, what a correct answer must satisfy and the output format, start zero-shot, and set the effort or thinking budget per task type. Then evaluate, because a prompt tuned for a chat model needs a fresh baseline.
When would you not use a reasoning model?

When the task is simple and latency-bound, such as a status lookup, a classification or a short reply: a non-reasoning model answers in under a second at a small fraction of the cost with similar accuracy. Also when you must audit a fixed procedure step by step; run those steps in code as a workflow and log each one, rather than hoping the hidden thinking follows it.
mis: Keeping “think step by step” and a numbered recipe in the prompt
State the goal, constraints and checks, and let the model plan its own path
Asking for the reasoning in the answer
Ask for the answer or JSON only; the thinking already happens, and is billed, in thinking tokens

longctx.t: A 2,50,000-token bundle costs ₹0.25 per 1,000 input tokens, and cached reads cost a tenth. Over 50 questions with caching (the first question pays in full), what is the average input cost per question in rupees?
longctx.a: First question ₹62.5; the other 49 pay ₹6.25 each = ₹306.25. Total ₹368.75 ÷ 50 = ₹7.375 a question, against ₹62.5 without caching.
iv: How would you prompt a model over a 300-page contract?

Put the contract first, split into tagged documents with source and page ranges, and the question last. Ask for the relevant quotes before the answer, and verify the quotes exist. Cache the prefix if several questions will be asked, and compare with retrieval on real multi-hop questions.
When is retrieval better than a long context?

When questions need a few passages from a large or changing corpus, when cost and latency per call matter, or when the documents exceed the context window. Long context wins when questions span many parts of one file and many questions share it.
mis: Putting the question above the documents
Place documents first and the question at the end
Re-sending the same documents at full price
Cache the shared prefix

mlprompt.t: 400 English messages score 95%, 300 Hinglish 90% and 300 Hindi 92% on intent. What is the overall accuracy, in percent?
iv: How do you design an extraction prompt for Hinglish users?
Keep keys and enum labels in English, state the reply language and script, add rules and examples for amounts and dates, include code-mixed examples, and report accuracy per language slice.
Should you translate user messages to English before the model?
Usually not: modern models read Hindi and Hinglish directly, and translation can mangle names, amounts and intent. Translate outputs when an English audit copy is needed.

gloss: system prompt
Standing instructions given to the model before the conversation: role, rules, tools and format.
few-shot prompting
Including a few input–output examples in the prompt to show the model what to do.
majority-label bias
A tendency to predict the label that appears most often in the examples.
recency bias
A tendency to copy the label of the last example shown.
JSON Schema
A standard way to describe the structure of JSON data: fields, types and constraints.
JSON mode
An API setting that guarantees syntactically valid JSON, without enforcing a schema.
structured outputs
An API mode where decoding is constrained so the output matches a given JSON Schema.
constrained decoding
Restricting which tokens the model can generate so the output follows a grammar or schema.
Pydantic
A Python library for defining data models with types and validators.
repair loop
Sending a validation error back to the model to get a corrected output, a limited number of times.
golden set
A curated set of real inputs with expected outputs or criteria, used to test prompt changes.
StrictUndefined
A Jinja2 setting that raises an error when a template variable is missing.
model tier
A size or capability level of model, such as small, medium or large, with matching price and speed.
compounding error
When each step’s errors carry into the next, so end-to-end accuracy is roughly the product of step accuracies.
reasoning effort
A per-request setting, such as low, medium or high, that tells a reasoning model roughly how much to think before answering.
thinking tokens
Tokens a reasoning model generates while working through a problem before its answer; billed as output tokens even when hidden or summarised.
prompt scaffold
Step-by-step instructions, such as “think step by step” and numbered procedures, that tell a model how to reason rather than what to achieve.
lost in the middle
The tendency of models to use information at the start or end of a long context more reliably than information in the middle.
quote-first prompting
Asking the model to extract the relevant passages before answering, so the answer rests on checkable quotes.
code-mixing
Switching between languages within one message, such as Hindi and English in Hinglish.
per-slice evaluation
Measuring accuracy separately for each group, such as each language, so a weak group is not hidden by the average.

sysprompt.name: Prompt Caching
sysprompt.note: Stable system-prompt text first and variables last is what makes prompt caching work.

templates.name: Prompt and Model Versioning
templates.note: Templates and regression tests make a prompt change safe to write; a registry and trace stamps make it safe to ship and roll back.

templates.name: System-Level Eval
templates.note: A golden-case suite for prompts is a system-level eval run on every change.

schema.name: Function Calling Basics
schema.note: Strict tool use applies the same schema guarantee to tool arguments that structured outputs give to answers.

schema.name: Plan-and-Execute
schema.note: A planner that returns a structured list of steps is far easier to execute and check than one that writes prose.

schema.name: Prompt vs RAG vs Fine-Tune
schema.note: Many format problems that seem to need fine-tuning are solved by strict structured outputs at no training cost.

schema.name: Pydantic AI
schema.note: Pydantic AI’s output types are strict structured outputs with a validation-and-retry loop built in.

schema.name: Multimodal Inputs
schema.note: Extract documents into a strict schema so vision-model output can be validated and cross-checked.

schema.name: Prompting Reasoning Models
schema.note: Asking a reasoning model for the answer only pairs naturally with structured outputs: the thinking stays in its own tokens and the reply is a schema-checked object.

schema.name: Multilingual Prompting (Hindi, Hinglish)
schema.note: Keep schema keys and enum values in English so outputs validate whatever language the user writes in.

repair.name: Output Guardrails
repair.note: A repair loop is an output rail that fixes rather than blocks: validate, send the error back, and escalate if it still fails.

repair.name: Model Routing and Tiering
repair.note: When validation keeps failing on a small model, a cascade escalates that request to a larger one; tiering picks the cheapest model that passes each step.

fewshot.name: LLM-as-a-Judge
fewshot.note: Few-shot examples in a judge prompt carry the same label and order biases, so calibrate judges on held-out labels.

fewshot.name: Supervised Fine-Tuning with LoRA and QLoRA
fewshot.note: Few-shot examples teach in the prompt on every call; fine-tuning bakes the same examples into the weights once, which pays off at high volume.

fewshot.name: Prompting Reasoning Models
fewshot.note: Few-shot examples help chat models with format and subtle labels; on reasoning models start zero-shot and add an example only when the format needs showing.

reasonprompt.name: Reasoning Models and Thinking Budgets
reasonprompt.note: Thinking budgets decide how much thinking to buy for each task; prompting reasoning models decides what the prompt around that thinking should say: goals and checks, not a step-by-step recipe.

reasonprompt.name: Few-Shot Examples
reasonprompt.note: Few-shot examples help chat models with format and subtle labels; on reasoning models start zero-shot and add an example only when the format needs showing.

reasonprompt.name: Model Routing and Tiering
reasonprompt.note: Routing sends each request to the cheapest model that can handle it; for reasoning models that means lookups go to a non-reasoning model and only multi-step tasks pay for thinking.

reasonprompt.name: JSON Schema and Constrained Decoding
reasonprompt.note: Asking a reasoning model for the answer only pairs naturally with structured outputs: the thinking stays in its own tokens and the reply is a schema-checked object.

longctx.name: Prompt Caching
longctx.note: Prompt caching turns a long shared document prefix from full price into a fraction on every later question.

longctx.name: Chunking Strategies
longctx.note: Retrieval with good chunks is the alternative when questions need only a few passages; compare both on your own questions.

longctx.name: Context Budgeting
longctx.note: A long document prefix eats the context budget; decide what stays in context and what is retrieved.

mlprompt.name: Multilingual and Code-Mixed Embeddings
mlprompt.note: Retrieval needs multilingual embeddings; the prompt needs rules for language, labels and amounts.

mlprompt.name: JSON Schema and Constrained Decoding
mlprompt.note: Keep schema keys and enum values in English so outputs validate whatever language the user writes in.

mlprompt.name: Speech in Indian Languages
mlprompt.note: Speech recognition produces the Hindi and Hinglish text that these prompts then have to handle.

gifs.fewshot: Five skewed examples make the model label 60% of complaints as refunds against a true 30%; one balanced example per label brings it back to 31%, and retrieved examples reach 91% accuracy.
gifs.longctx: A long prompt holds three tagged loan documents, about 2,50,000 tokens, with a cached prefix. The question sits at the end. The model first quotes the prepayment clauses from the agreement and the 2025 addendum, then answers from the quotes. Accuracy on 50 questions rises from 80 to 89 percent and the cost per question falls from about ₹63 to about ₹8.
gifs.mlprompt: A Hinglish message asks when a ₹3,500 refund will arrive. The model returns JSON with English keys and an English intent label, the amount normalised to 3500, and replies in Hinglish. Intent accuracy on Hinglish messages rises from 78 to 90 percent once code-mixed examples are added.
gifs.reasonprompt: An animated scene for RupeeRail, a fictional payment aggregator, running 10,000 tasks a day on a reasoning model. First a prompt card shows a chat-model scaffold in red: think step by step, numbered steps, five worked examples and show all your working; beside it, reconciliations are 89% right, the day costs ₹41,948 and lookups take 21.4 seconds at the 95th percentile. The prompt then changes to green lines stating the goal, the rules, one check and "reply with the JSON only": reconciliations rise to 93% and the cost falls to ₹36,295, while lookups still take 19.2 seconds. Finally two lanes appear: 7,000 lookups go to a fast model with no thinking and 3,000 reconciliations go to the reasoning model at high effort; the cost falls to ₹25,900 a day, lookups answer in 0.7 seconds, and overall accuracy is 96.2%.
gifs.repair: 17 of 100 invoices break a business rule; sending the exact error back leaves 5 after one repair and under 2 after two, and those go to a human queue while clean records reach the ledger.
gifs.schema: With a prompt asking for JSON, 7 of 100 outputs fail to parse and 8 miss fields; a strict schema fixes the shape of all 100, but 9 still carry wrong values.
gifs.sysprompt: A vague one-paragraph prompt handles 66% of tickets; rewritten in clear sections with rules, tool guidance, format and a fallback it handles 90%, and putting data last lets 90% of the prompt be cached.
gifs.templates: A strict template turns a missing variable into a test failure; a golden suite of 20, 100 or 300 cases catches a change that breaks a 3% intent 46%, 95% or over 99% of the time, and CI blocks the merge.

header.lede: The cheapest, highest-leverage skill in agent engineering: tell the model clearly what to do, show it well-chosen examples, force its output into a shape your code can trust, repair what still goes wrong, and keep prompts under test. Choosing the smallest model for each step is covered under Model Routing in Cost Optimisation.
